planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or nursery plugs in spring into loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; this low mat-forming verbena roots at the nodes as it creeps, so a few starter plants fill in quickly along a sunny coastal bed edge.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings or plugs into loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; this Florida dune native forms a dense, glossy mat of toothed foliage studded with deep pink to lavender flower clusters that bloom nearly year-round in mild Gulf Coast winters. Once its roots reach moisture reserves it needs no supplemental irrigation and shrugs off salt spray and blowing sand, making it a good choice for stabilizing loose soil along a sunny walkway or coastal border. The nectar-rich blooms draw bees, butterflies, and moths through the long warm season, and the trailing stems can be trimmed back hard in late winter to keep growth tidy.

planting.note: Direct sow or set out small starts in spring into loose, sandy or shelly soil in full sun; this low mint-family herb self-sows readily on disturbed sandy ground and short-lived plants are usually replaced by their own seedlings within a season or two.

directions: Sow directly into loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; small coastal germander is a diminutive, aromatic mint-family annual to short-lived perennial found on coastal sands and shell middens from Texas and Louisiana to Florida. Its lobed gray-green leaves and tiny white to pale blue speckled flowers stay low and inconspicuous, making it best suited to a sunny gravel path, dune restoration planting, or the gaps between coastal paving stones rather than a formal bed. It tolerates the long, humid Gulf Coast growing season without irrigation once established and self-sows into bare sandy patches, filling niches too dry and infertile for most other groundcovers.

planting.note: Direct sow in spring onto sandy or shelly ground in full sun near the salt line; this small annual succulent completes its life cycle in one warm season and readily reseeds itself on bare, salty ground each year.

directions: Scatter seed directly onto sandy or shelly, saline soil in full sun and keep lightly moist only until seedlings establish; this small, fleshy-leaved annual is the shorter-lived cousin of the more familiar trailing sea purslane and naturally colonizes the upper edges of salt flats, brackish pond margins, and open sandy beach soil along the Gulf. Its thick reddish stems and tiny pink flowers form a low mat that tolerates salinity most garden plants cannot survive, so it earns a place at the salty, sun-baked fringe of a coastal planting bed where nothing else will grow. Because it is a true annual, expect it to complete its cycle and drop seed within a single hot Gulf Coast summer, then return the following year from that seed bank.

planting.note: Direct sow or plant divisions in spring into loose, sandy, well-drained soil in full sun; the spreading underground stolons form a sparse patch over time, so give it open sandy ground rather than a crowded bed.

directions: Plant into loose, well-drained sandy soil in full sun, where its tuberous roots and underground stolons let it persist through drought and sandy, nutrient-poor conditions typical of Gulf Coast dunes and coastal scrub. The nodding yellow, trumpet-shaped flowers give way to small yellow fruits enclosed in a papery lantern husk, similar in form to a garden ground cherry but produced by a true native of Gulf shoreline habitat from Texas to Florida. It dies back in cooler winters further inland but stays evergreen in the mildest coastal zones, resprouting reliably each spring to take advantage of the long, hot growing season. Use it in a naturalized coastal bed or dune-edge planting where its sprawling habit and light fruit set are more curiosity than crop, though the ripe fruit is edible.
sources: University of South Florida Atlas of Florida Plants

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring into moist to wet, brackish or sandy soil in full sun; this fast-growing shrub establishes quickly along ditches, pond edges, and low spots that flood with brackish water after storms.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs into moist, brackish, or occasionally flooded soil in full sun; saltwater false willow is a fast-growing, upright native shrub of Gulf and South Atlantic coastal marshes with narrow, slightly succulent leaves that tolerate salt spray and fluctuating soil salinity better than most woody plants. It is dioecious, with male and female flowers on separate plants, and produces small tufted seed heads in fall that support pollinating insects late in the season. Because it thrives in the low, wet, salt-influenced spots where many landscape shrubs fail, it is a practical screening or erosion-control choice along the back edge of a Gulf Coast property near a ditch, pond, or brackish waterway. It tolerates hard pruning if a denser, shorter form is wanted.

planting.note: Direct sow or root stem cuttings in spring into loose, dry, sandy soil in full sun; the trailing stems root wherever they touch sand, so a small planting spreads into a full groundcover mat within a season.

directions: Plant into loose, dry, sandy soil in full sun and avoid overwatering, which quickly rots this short-lived dune perennial; coastal ragweed forms a low, bushy, deeply lobed mat that roots at the stem nodes as it spreads, making it useful for stabilizing loose sand on a beachfront lot or open coastal bed where little else will take hold. It thrives in the intense heat, salt spray, and drought of a Gulf Coast summer and needs essentially no supplemental care once rooted in appropriate sandy ground. Because it produces abundant wind-borne pollen, site it away from patios, windows, and other areas where people spend time outdoors, and reserve it for dune stabilization or the far edges of the landscape rather than near the house.
sources: University of South Florida Atlas of Florida Plants

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown clumps in spring into moist to seasonally wet, sandy soil in full sun; established clumps expand slowly outward and rarely need division once sited in a low, damp spot.

directions: Plant divisions or nursery clumps into moist, sandy soil in full sun, in a wetland margin, pond edge, or seasonally damp low spot; sand cordgrass forms tight, fountain-like clumps of fine arching blades that tolerate both standing brackish water and drier upland sand once roots are established, unlike its rhizomatous cordgrass relatives that spread aggressively along tidal shorelines. It stays evergreen through mild Gulf Coast winters and provides cover for marsh birds and small wildlife while its dense root mass helps stabilize pond banks and low drainage areas against erosion. Use it as a substitute for non-native ornamental grasses in a rain garden, retention pond edge, or naturalized wet meadow planting where its clumping habit will not overrun neighboring plants.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension EDIS
University of Florida/IFAS Center for Land Use Efficiency

planting.note: Direct sow or set out small starts in spring into sandy, saline to alkaline soil in full sun; this sprawling succulent groundcover spreads by branching stems and tolerates both salty flats and dry sandy ground once established.

directions: Sow directly or plant starts into sandy, saline, or alkaline soil in full sun; seaside heliotrope is a sprawling, fleshy-leaved native groundcover with a powdery bluish-gray cast that tolerates salt flats, brackish waste ground, and dry coastal sand where few other flowering plants persist. Small white flowers with yellow throats open along gradually uncoiling, scorpion-tail flower spikes from spring through fall, drawing a steady stream of native bees and butterflies through the long warm Gulf Coast season. It thrives with minimal watering once rooted and is well suited to a hot, dry parking strip, gravel bed, or salt-affected low spot near a coastal driveway where turf and typical bedding plants struggle.
